the primary tumor should be removed if the patient has no evidence of metastatic disease.

the development of new methods for the detection and removal of cancer.
the role of the primary tumor and the effect of surgical removal on survival in patients with metastatic disease.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the data presented by Flanigan and colleagues1 support the use of nephrectomy as a treatment for patients with metastatic renal cancer who have a solitary metastasis, but the data are insufficient to support this procedure in patients with multiple metastases.
the data do not support the practice of removing the primary tumor in most patients with metastatic cancer.

the removal of the primary cancer in patients with metastatic disease should be performed only when the primary tumor is causing significant symptoms or when the removal of the tumor will significantly alter the course of the disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to the management of patients with renal cancer and have provided a rationale for a new treatment paradigm in the management of patients in whom the primary tumor has been removed but who already have evidence that their disease has spread.
we have shown that the primary tumor is a source of metastatic tumor cells and that removal of the tumor may reduce the number of metastases in some patients.
the results of surgery for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) in the metastatic setting are better than expected and that surgery can be safely performed.

we need to do a better job of educating the public about cancer.
